triage.name: Concussion
triage.reason: Common head injury with characteristic history and exam; diagnosis reachable clinically with important red flags to exclude.

presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

age.peak: bimodal: adolescents/young adults (15–25) and older adults (65+)

demographics: More common in males, especially adolescents and young adults, reflecting higher rates of contact sports and risk-taking injuries
Older adults have higher rates of concussion from falls, often with more severe consequences
Children and adolescents are frequently affected, particularly in organized sports

risk_factors.text: Participation in contact or collision sports (e.g., football, soccer, hockey, basketball)
History of falls or gait instability

comorbidities: Coagulopathy or anticoagulant use (increases risk of intracranial hemorrhage)
exposures: Rapid acceleration-deceleration forces (e.g., whiplash, blast injury)

chief_complaints.text: I hit my head and now I have a headache

hpi.onset: Sudden, immediately after a blow to the head or body; symptoms may not be noticed until hours later
hpi.duration: Symptoms typically last days to weeks; most resolve within 7–10 days but can persist for months
hpi.progression: Symptoms begin immediately or within hours; may worsen over the first 24–48 hours, then gradually improve
hpi.location: Headache is usually generalized or frontal; neck pain may be present
hpi.radiation: Headache may radiate to the neck or behind the eyes
hpi.quality: Headache is typically pressure-like or throbbing; dizziness is described as lightheadedness or a spinning sensation
hpi.severity: Variable; headache often moderate (4–7/10), but can be severe
hpi.timing: Headache is often constant, worsened by physical or cognitive exertion
relieving: Rest in a dark, quiet room
Acetaminophen or ibuprofen (may help headache but must be used cautiously)

associated_symptoms.text: Feeling mentally foggy or slowed down
Sleep disturbances (sleeping more or less than usual)
Loss of consciousness (brief, seconds to minutes)

pertinent_negatives: Loss of consciousness lasting more than a few minutes
Weakness or numbness in arms or legs
Clear fluid or blood from nose or ears

argues_against: Focal neurological deficit suggests structural brain injury (e.g., hemorrhage, stroke)
Repeated vomiting suggests increased intracranial pressure

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may not report headache or dizziness; they may present with irritability, crying, vomiting, changes in sleep or eating, loss of interest in toys, or unsteady walking. They may be unable to describe amnesia or confusion.

Older adults may have subtle symptoms, and concussion can mimic dementia or delirium. They are at higher risk of intracranial hemorrhage, so a lower threshold for imaging is used. Symptoms like headache may be less prominent, while confusion or balance problems may dominate.
Infants may present with inconsolable crying, vomiting, poor feeding, lethargy, or irritability. A history of trauma may be absent or unclear. Non-accidental trauma should be considered.

general.mild: Alert, oriented, appears well; may be slightly slowed or uncomfortable but not toxic
general.moderate: Dazed or foggy, mild distress, may be photophobic or holding head
general.severe: Ill-appearing, drowsy but arousable, may vomit or have significant headache
general.critical: Lethargic, difficult to arouse, focal deficits, or signs of herniation (e.g., unequal pupils, posturing)

imaging.preferred_when: Moderate or severe head injury, GCS <15, focal deficit, anticoagulation, or high-risk mechanism; not needed for most mild concussions

findings.text: No acute intracranial abnormality (normal study, the expected result in uncomplicated concussion)
Small intracranial hemorrhage (epidural, subdural, subarachnoid, or intraparenchymal)
Diffuse cerebral edema or mass effect with midline shift

imaging.preferred_when: Persistent or worsening symptoms, or when CT is normal but a structural cause is still suspected

findings.text: Normal study in most patients with concussion
Small areas of signal abnormality consistent with axonal injury or microhemorrhage
Extra-axial fluid collection or contusion not seen on CT

imaging.preferred_when: Midline neck tenderness, focal neurologic deficit, or high-risk mechanism with concern for cervical injury

findings.text: Usually normal; not sensitive for intracranial injury

initial.why: Excludes intracranial hemorrhage or fracture in patients with red flags or high-risk features
initial.only_if: moderate or severe head injury, GCS <15, focal neurologic deficit, anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, suspected skull fracture, or high-risk mechanism
midline neck tenderness, focal deficit, or high-risk mechanism

supporting.why: May show structural injury when symptoms persist or worsen despite a normal CT
supporting.only_if: persistent or worsening symptoms with a normal CT

not_indicated.why: Not routinely needed; no blood abnormality defines concussion
Not routinely needed unless there is vomiting, poor intake, or another indication
Not needed unless bleeding risk or anticoagulation is being assessed
Less sensitive than CT and rarely changes management

decision_points: Use a validated decision rule to decide whether head CT is needed in mild injury
Do not delay CT in patients with focal deficits, worsening mental status, or suspected skull fracture
Consider cervical spine imaging when neck tenderness or a high-risk mechanism is present
Pregnancy test before CT in anyone who could be pregnant

criteria.name: Concussion (mild traumatic brain injury)
criteria.summary: A clinical diagnosis after a blow to the head or body causing rapid brain movement, with one or more of: confusion or disorientation, brief loss of consciousness, amnesia around the event, or other transient neurologic symptoms, in a patient with a normal or near-normal Glasgow Coma Scale and no structural injury on imaging.
items: Blunt head trauma or acceleration-deceleration force
Transient confusion, disorientation, or impaired awareness
Brief loss of consciousness (seconds to minutes)
Amnesia for events before or after the injury
Headache, dizziness, nausea, balance problems, or visual symptoms
No structural intracranial injury on imaging when imaging is performed

differential.name: Epidural hematoma
differential.why_considered: Head trauma with headache and altered mental status; can mimic concussion but is a structural emergency.
differential.trigger: Brief loss of consciousness followed by a lucid interval then rapid deterioration, or focal neurologic deficit after head trauma.

history: Brief loss of consciousness followed by a lucid interval then rapid decline
Severe, progressively worsening headache
Vomiting
exam: Focal neurologic deficit (e.g., hemiparesis, pupillary asymmetry)
Signs of herniation (e.g., ipsilateral pupil dilation, contralateral hemiparesis)
imaging: CT head shows a biconvex (lentiform) extra-axial collection, often with midline shift

differential.name: Subdural hematoma
differential.why_considered: Head trauma with headache and confusion, especially in older adults or those on anticoagulants.
differential.trigger: Head trauma in an older adult or anticoagulated patient, with headache, confusion, or focal deficit.

history: Head trauma, which may be minor or unwitnessed
Gradual onset of confusion, headache, or weakness over hours to days
Anticoagulant or antiplatelet use
exam: Signs of increased intracranial pressure (e.g., papilledema, bradycardia, hypertension)
labs: Coagulation studies may show prolonged INR or elevated aPTT if on anticoagulants
imaging: CT head shows a crescent-shaped extra-axial collection, often with midline shift

differential.name: Subarachnoid hemorrhage
differential.why_considered: Sudden severe headache after trauma or spontaneous onset, which can be mistaken for post-concussive headache.
differential.trigger: Thunderclap headache (sudden, severe) or headache with neck stiffness and vomiting.

history: Sudden onset of severe headache (thunderclap)
Neck pain or stiffness
Nausea and vomiting
May have brief loss of consciousness
exam: Focal neurologic deficit if associated with aneurysm
imaging: CT head shows hyperdense blood in subarachnoid spaces (e.g., basal cisterns, sulci)
If CT is negative but suspicion remains, lumbar puncture shows xanthochromia

differential.name: Cervical spine injury
differential.why_considered: Head trauma often involves the neck; neck pain and tenderness can be attributed to concussion but may indicate fracture or ligamentous injury.
differential.trigger: Midline neck tenderness, focal neurologic deficit, or high-risk mechanism.

history: Neck pain after trauma
High-risk mechanism (e.g., diving, motor vehicle collision)
Focal neurologic symptoms in arms or legs
exam: Focal neurologic deficit (e.g., weakness, sensory loss, hyperreflexia)
imaging: Cervical spine CT shows fracture or subluxation
MRI may show ligamentous injury or spinal cord compression

differential.name: Post-traumatic migraine
differential.why_considered: Headache after head trauma can be migrainous, especially in patients with a personal or family history of migraine.

history: Personal or family history of migraine
Headache is throbbing, often unilateral, with nausea and light/sound sensitivity
May have aura

differential.name: Acute stress reaction
differential.why_considered: After a traumatic event, patients may have dizziness, headache, and difficulty concentrating due to psychological distress.

history: Symptoms are temporally linked to stress or emotional trigger
No direct head impact or the impact was trivial
Symptoms may include palpitations, sweating, tremor
exam: Signs of anxiety (e.g., tachycardia, tremulousness) without focal deficits

differential.name: Vestibular disorder (e.g., BPPV)
differential.why_considered: Dizziness and imbalance after head trauma can be due to peripheral vestibular causes, especially if positional.

history: Brief episodes of vertigo triggered by head position changes
No headache or cognitive symptoms
May have a history of similar episodes
exam: Dix-Hallpike maneuver reproduces vertigo with nystagmus

severity.mild: Symptoms are mild and do not interfere with daily activities; headache is mild, no confusion, no loss of consciousness, and the patient is fully oriented.
severity.moderate: Symptoms are moderate and interfere with some activities; headache is moderate, may have some confusion or amnesia, but the patient is hemodynamically stable and neurologically intact.
severity.severe: Symptoms are severe and prevent normal activities; severe headache, repeated vomiting, significant confusion, or focal neurologic deficits may be present, but the patient is not in a coma.
severity.critical: The patient has a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 8 or less, signs of herniation (e.g., unequal pupils, posturing), or requires immediate neurosurgical intervention; this represents a severe traumatic brain injury, not a simple concussion.

red_flags.meaning: May indicate increased intracranial pressure or a structural lesion.
Could signal intracranial hemorrhage or expanding mass.

red_flags.finding: Focal neurologic deficit (e.g., weakness, numbness, slurred speech)
red_flags.meaning: Suggests a structural brain injury such as hemorrhage or stroke.
Indicates a more severe brain injury or underlying condition.

red_flags.finding: Loss of consciousness lasting more than a few minutes
red_flags.meaning: Suggests a more severe traumatic brain injury.

red_flags.finding: Unequal pupils or sluggish pupillary response
red_flags.meaning: Sign of herniation or brainstem compression.

red_flags.finding: Clear fluid or blood from the nose or ears
red_flags.meaning: Suggests basilar skull fracture with CSF leak.

red_flags.finding: Inability to wake up or extreme drowsiness
red_flags.meaning: Indicates severe brain injury or increased intracranial pressure.

complications.name: Post-concussion syndrome
clues: Symptoms such as headache, dizziness, and difficulty concentrating persist for weeks to months after the injury
Symptoms are exacerbated by physical or cognitive exertion

complications.name: Second impact syndrome
clues: A second head injury occurs before the first concussion has resolved
Rapid onset of severe symptoms, including loss of consciousness, seizures, or respiratory failure

complications.name: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy
clues: History of multiple concussions, often in contact sports
Progressive cognitive decline, mood changes, and behavioral disturbances years after injuries

complications.name: Post-traumatic epilepsy
clues: Seizures occurring weeks to years after the head injury

special_populations.differences: Young children may not report headache or dizziness; they may present with irritability, crying, vomiting, changes in sleep or eating, loss of interest in toys, or unsteady walking. They may be unable to describe amnesia or confusion. Non-accidental trauma should be considered if the history is inconsistent with the injury.

Older adults may have subtle symptoms, and concussion can mimic dementia or delirium. They are at higher risk of intracranial hemorrhage, so a lower threshold for imaging is used. Symptoms like headache may be less prominent, while confusion or balance problems may dominate.
Infants may present with inconsolable crying, vomiting, poor feeding, lethargy, or irritability. A history of trauma may be absent or unclear. Non-accidental trauma should be considered.

key_questions.question: What happened? Did you hit your head or have a blow to the body?
key_questions.looking_for: A blunt head impact or a rapid acceleration-deceleration event such as a fall, collision, or whiplash

key_questions.question: Did you lose consciousness? If so, for how long?
key_questions.looking_for: Brief loss of consciousness (seconds to a minute) or none at all; longer than a few minutes suggests more severe injury

key_questions.question: Do you remember what happened right before and right after the injury?
key_questions.looking_for: Amnesia for events before or after the impact, which supports the diagnosis

key_questions.question: Were you confused, dazed, or 'not yourself' right after the hit?
key_questions.looking_for: Transient confusion or disorientation immediately after the injury

key_questions.question: When did your symptoms start?
key_questions.looking_for: Immediately after the injury, though some symptoms may not be noticed for hours

key_questions.question: What makes your symptoms worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Physical exertion, mental concentration, bright lights, loud noises, or rapid head movements

key_questions.question: Have you had a concussion or head injury before?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior concussion, which increases risk and can prolong recovery

key_questions.question: Do you take any blood thinners or antiplatelet medicines?
key_questions.looking_for: Anticoagulants (warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban) or antiplatelet agents (aspirin, clopidogrel), which raise the risk of intracranial bleeding

key_questions.question: Have you vomited? How many times?
key_questions.looking_for: One episode may occur with concussion; repeated vomiting is a red flag for increased intracranial pressure

key_questions.question: Do you have any weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, or trouble walking?
key_questions.looking_for: Focal neurologic deficits, which suggest a structural brain injury rather than simple concussion

key_questions.question: Is your headache getting worse over time, or is it the worst headache of your life?
key_questions.looking_for: A progressively worsening or thunderclap headache, which raises concern for hemorrhage

key_questions.question: Have you had any seizures or convulsions?
key_questions.looking_for: Seizure activity, which indicates a more severe brain injury

key_questions.question: Is there any clear fluid or blood coming from your nose or ears?
key_questions.looking_for: CSF leak or bleeding, suggesting a basilar skull fracture

key_questions.question: Do you have neck pain, especially in the middle of the back of your neck?
key_questions.looking_for: Midline cervical tenderness, which may indicate a cervical spine injury

key_questions.question: Are you having trouble with your vision, like blurriness or double vision?
key_questions.looking_for: Visual symptoms such as blurred or double vision, which are common after concussion

key_questions.question: How is your sleep? Are you sleeping more or less than usual?
key_questions.looking_for: Sleep disturbances, which are common after concussion

key_questions.question: Do you play any contact sports or have you had a recent fall?
key_questions.looking_for: Athletic participation or fall risk, which helps identify the mechanism and risk of recurrence

reasoning_points: A blunt head trauma or acceleration-deceleration force occurred
Transient confusion, disorientation, or impaired awareness was present after the injury
Brief loss of consciousness or amnesia around the event may have occurred
Symptoms such as headache, dizziness, nausea, balance problems, or visual changes are present
Glasgow Coma Scale is 13-15 with no focal neurologic deficit
No structural intracranial injury is seen on imaging when imaging is performed
Red flags for more severe injury (repeated vomiting, worsening headache, focal deficits, seizure, prolonged loss of consciousness) are absent

easy: Adolescent athlete with a clear blow to the head during a game
Brief confusion or dazed appearance witnessed by others
Headache, dizziness, and nausea that worsen with exertion
medium: Older adult who fell and now has confusion and balance problems without a clear headache
Patient on an anticoagulant with a minor head strike and mild symptoms
Symptoms that began hours after the injury rather than immediately
Neck pain accompanying the head injury, requiring cervical spine assessment
hard: Young child with irritability, vomiting, and poor feeding but no clear history of trauma
Patient with pre-existing migraine or ADHD whose symptoms are attributed to those conditions
Older adult with subtle cognitive changes mistaken for dementia or delirium
Patient with a normal head CT but persistent symptoms raising concern for another diagnosis
